youtube.title: Why Do We Have Seasons? Day, Night and Earth's Tilt for Kids | Grade 4 Science | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Is the Sun moving, or are we? Robo, Owl and Penguin build a model with a tilted globe and a sun lamp.
Kids learn that Earth spins on its axis about once every 24 hours (day and night), why shadows are long in the morning and evening and short at noon, that one orbit around the Sun takes about 365¼ days (and why we have leap days), and that the seasons come from Earth's 23.5° tilt, not from distance: Penguin's December summer and Earth being closest to the Sun in January are the evidence.
Try at home: a shadow stick (mark the shadow tip in the morning, at noon and in the afternoon) and a flashlight on squared paper. Never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses; don't shine a flashlight into anyone's eyes; and ask a grown-up to set up a desk lamp, because bulbs get hot.

Spin = 1 day: day and night.
Orbit = 1 year: about 365¼ days.
Tilt = the seasons: direct light and long days.
Not distance! The south has winter when the north has summer.
Shadow stick: stand a pencil in clay on paper outside. Mark the shadow tip in the morning, at noon and in the afternoon. Which is shortest?

do.text: Spinning Earth
Look! The Sun comes up in the east, runs across the sky, and goes down in the west.
The Sun runs round us every day!
Does it? Or are we the ones moving?
Let's build a model and look for evidence.
This lamp is our Sun. This globe is our Earth.
Earth spins around an imaginary line called the axis.
It goes through the North and South Poles.
axis: North Pole to South Pole
The axis is tilted. It leans about twenty three and a half degrees.
tilt: 23.5°
And it always points the same way, toward the North Star.
The real Sun is about one hundred nine times wider than Earth.
And it is about one hundred fifty million kilometres away.
Model not to scale
This red dot is my town.
Right now it's on the dark side, facing away from the Sun. It's night.
Half of Earth is always lit. The other half is in darkness.
Earth spins toward the east. Where will the town be at noon?
Sunrise! The town turns into the light. The Sun seems to come up in the east.
sunrise
Noon. The town faces the Sun. It's the middle of the day.
noon
Sunset. The town turns away. The Sun seems to go down in the west.
sunset
Night again. One full spin takes about twenty four hours. One day!
night
So the Sun only looks like it moves, because we spin!
Evidence: the lamp never moved.
1 spin = about 24 hours
Fun fact:
at the equator, the ground spins at about one thousand six hundred seventy kilometres per hour!
Let's zoom in on the town. A stick stands in the ground.
Shadows always point away from the light.
Morning. The Sun is low in the east. The shadow is long, and points west.
Where will the shadow be at noon? Long or short?
Noon. The Sun is high. The shadow is short!
Evening. The Sun is low in the west. The shadow is long again, and points east.
Long, short, long. Because Earth spins, the Sun seems to cross the sky.
long · short · long
Earth does not only spin. It also travels around the Sun. That trip is called an orbit.
Watch the globe go once around the lamp. The path is nearly a circle.
365¼ days
One trip around the Sun takes about three hundred sixty five and a quarter days.
One year!
1 orbit = 1 year
And Earth spins about three hundred sixty five times on the way. Too fast to count here!
Those extra quarter days add up.
So every four years, we add a leap day: the twenty ninth of February.
leap day: 29 February
I know why we have summer! Summer is when Earth is closest to the Sun.
That sounds sensible. Let's check the evidence.
Hello! I live far in the south. At my home, December is summer!
And in December, it is winter in the north. Same Earth, same distance from the Sun.
Oh. Both halves are the same distance away, but they have opposite seasons.
Evidence two. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
That's winter in the north! So distance can't be the reason.
So what does make the seasons? A flashlight test. First, shine the light straight down.
The spot covers about four squares. It looks bright.
Now tilt the light. How many squares will the same light cover?
About eight squares!
The same light is spread out, so each square gets about half as much.
Direct light warms more. Slanted light warms less.
direct light: warmer · slanted light: cooler
Now the four stops around the Sun. Watch the axis. It always points at the North Star.
June. The north half leans toward the Sun.
Direct light and long days. Summer in the north!
June: summer in the north
And winter in the south, because the south half leans away.
September. Neither half leans toward the Sun. Autumn in the north, spring in the south.
September: autumn in the north
December. Now the north half leans away.
Slanted light and short days. Winter in the north.
December: winter in the north
And summer for me in the south! In December, the Sun never sets at the South Pole.
March. Neither half leans toward the Sun again.
Spring in the north, autumn in the south.
March: spring in the north
Places near the equator get fairly direct light all year, so their seasons change less.
So the tilt makes the seasons, not the distance. That's the big idea!
tilt → seasons
Spin for the day!
Go round for the year!
Lean to the Sun, and summer is here!
Spin makes?
Spin makes?
Day and night!
Trip makes?
Trip makes?
A year!
Tilt makes?
Tilt makes?
Seasons!
Stand up, lean a little, and turn slowly on the spot. You are Earth!
One: The Sun goes round Earth every day. True or false?
False. Earth spins. The Sun only looks like it moves.
Two: Earth spins once about every 24 hours. True or false?
True. One spin is one day.
Three: It is summer in the north when Earth is closest to the Sun. True or false?
False. Earth is closest in January, during northern winter.
Four: When it is summer in the north, it is winter in the south. True or false?
True. The halves lean the opposite way.
Five: Your shadow is shortest around noon. True or false?
True. The Sun is highest then.
Quiz time! One: what causes day and night?
Earth spinning on its axis.
Two: how long does Earth take to go once round the Sun?
About three hundred sixty five and a quarter days. One year.
Three: why is it summer in the north in June?
The north half leans toward the Sun. More direct light and longer days.
Four: is summer caused by being closer to the Sun? What's your evidence?
No! The south has winter at the same time, and Earth is closest in January.
Spin makes day and night. One orbit makes a year.
The tilt makes the seasons. Not distance!
Bye from the south!
And hello from the north. The evidence agrees!
Your turn! On a sunny day, stand a pencil in clay on paper.
Mark the shadow tip three times.
Never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses.
Don't shine a flashlight in anyone's eyes.
Never look at the Sun!
Using a desk lamp as the Sun? Ask a grown-up to set it up. Bulbs get hot.
Spin for the day, go round for the year. Bye, space explorers!
